All three claimed sub-clauses are textually present: (1) compare each listed timestamp against the run-slug pointer's own timestamp in the same listing (line 276-277), (2) treat an older file as not this run's (line 277, verbatim), (3) do this before any re-entry (line 276, 'Before any re-entry'). SEPARATE substantive concern (not part of the textual claim's truth value, but worth flagging): the surrounding text specifies a plain 'ls -l' invocation with no format flags. Default `ls -l` timestamp granularity on both GNU coreutils and BSD ls is one minute for files modified within the recent-time window (only switching to a coarser year granularity for older files, never finer than minutes) -- there is no seconds-level default output. Since the four listed files (issue-run-slug pointer, issue-step1, issue-derivation, issue-audit) are plausibly all written within the same run, often within the same minute, an 'older than the pointer' comparison at minute granularity can fail to discriminate true creation order for files written seconds apart, meaning ties (same-minute timestamps) are not disambiguated by the instruction -- files written in the same minute as the pointer would compare as equal-age rather than newer, so the intended older-than-pointer check may under-detect a stale file from a prior run if that prior run's write happened to land in the same clock minute as the current pointer's write (unlikely but architecturally possible, e.g. clock skew or very fast successive runs). This is a design-robustness observation about the instruction's method, not a mismatch between the claim's wording and the instruction's text.

skills/create-issue/SKILL.md:283-286 reads: 'That single invocation's own output carries every outcome. A diagnostic naming a listed path, against the invocation's non-zero status, is an absent file; every other outcome — a missing command binary and a refused command alike — is reported unestablished and re-enters no producing step.' Probed the mixed present/absent case directly (scratch dir under /private/tmp/.../probe): `ls -l present1.md present2.md absent1.md absent2.md` prints both the listing lines for present files and 'ls: absentN.md: No such file or directory' diagnostics for absent ones on stdout/stderr of that one invocation — so for the absent-file and (shell-level) missing-command-binary cases, the invocation genuinely does produce output that carries the outcome (a stderr diagnostic distinguishable from a listing line). But the universal explicitly also folds in 'a refused command' as an outcome the same single invocation's output is claimed to carry. A harness refusal (the exact family CLAUDE.md's own 'SKILL.md bang injection limits' gotcha and the anchor-ladder bullet describe: 'A tool-level refusal leaves the channel *unestablished*', and the bang-injection case where the load 'returns an is_error result whose whole content is a permission-refusal string and no skill body at all') means the `ls -l` process is never executed by the shell at all — the harness denies the tool call pre-execution. In that case there is no stdout, no stderr, nothing the `ls -l` process itself emitted — i.e. no 'invocation's own output' exists to carry anything, because the invocation did not run. What the agent receives instead (if anything) is a permission-system message about the Bash tool call, not output of `ls -l`. So the sentence's own second clause is right to route the refused-command case to 'reported unestablished', but the first sentence's premise ('that single invocation's own output carries every outcome') is false precisely for that case: an outcome that produces literally no invocation output cannot be 'carried' by that output. The universal is self-contradicted by the very case its next clause enumerates.
